title: Reverse String (Recursion)
directAnswer: Base case: empty or single-char string returns itself. Recursive case: `reverse(s[1:]) + s[0]`.

remember.takeaway: String recursion: solve the tail, then attach the head.

problemStatement: Given a string `s`, return it reversed, using recursion.
understanding: Reverse the rest of the string, then append the first character — or swap ends moving inward.

approaches.name: Reverse-rest + prepend-first
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Reverse by recursion: reverse everything after the first character, then put the first character at the **end**. Base case is a string of length ≤ 1, which is its own reverse.

**Why append the head at the end.** `reverse(s[1:]) + s[0]` reverses the tail and tacks the original first character on after it — which places it last, exactly where a reversal sends it. Prepending instead would not reverse anything.

**Why this naive version is O(n²).** Each call builds a new string by concatenation, copying O(n) characters, across n calls → O(n²) time plus O(n) stack. The efficient form swaps characters in a char array with two indices moving inward (O(n) time, in place) — mention it as the upgrade.

Recursion here is a teaching device; iteration (two-pointer swap) is what you'd ship.
hints: Reverse the tail, then where does the first character go?
Why is the naive concatenation version O(n²)?
approaches.complexityReasoning: n recursive calls each concatenating O(n) characters → O(n²); the char-swap form is O(n).

java.explanation: Reverse the tail, then append the head.

pitfalls: Appending the first char at the front instead of the end.

commonMistakes: Appending the first char at the front instead of the end.
patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Reverse-rest + append-first. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.
